story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built PetnTrip because every time I booked a hotel with a dog or cat, I'd end up with multiple tabs open — one to check if "pet friendly" actually meant anything specific (fees, weight limits), one for reviews to see if it was enforced in practice.

It pulls pet policy details, Agoda ratings, and guest review highlights into one page per hotel, organized by city. Currently covers South Korea in depth, with a handful of US cities (LA, NYC, SF) so far.

Tech stack: Next.js (App Router/RSC), Supabase/Postgres, deployed on Vercel. Bookings route through Agoda, so I get a small affiliate commission there.

https://petntrip.aeihi.com/en

Would love feedback, especially on what's missing for US coverage.

story_text.value:
tl;dr: tilion is building the world's fastest and stealthiest browser infra for agents, so you can run millions of web agents successfully. today, we're releasing v3 of our engine, fortress, free for devs.

https://github.com/tiliondev/fortress

launch vid:

i am arham, cto of tilion (ycf26), and we (arman, abdul, and fardin) are building browser infra for agents.

before tilion, we were running thousands of web agents to collect multimodal school board data across the web. our agents kept getting blocked: cloudflare, akamai, captchas, and 200s that were actually empty pages. so we dug into chromium itself.

what we found:

- sites fingerprint the browser in about 40 places (gpu, canvas, fonts, timezone, and so on). a real machine is consistent in all of them, unlike a program-driven browser.

- plugins like puppeteer-stealth and undetected-chromedriver mostly patch from javascript, and the patch itself is detectable. (the irony)

- residential proxies fix the ip, but they're expensive. and if the fingerprint is wrong, you get blocked anyway. so we built and open sourced fortress.

our latest build has 81+ patches in c++. if an anti-bot system checks the browser, it all green-lights on its end.

in practice that means:

- you have higher success rates against blocks. - your proxy bill drops by half. - your agents can do more shit.

theres also a cli and mcp so you can get setup fast. we have windows, mac, and linux native builds. we'll also be launching our cloud browsers, for which we are running millions of agents every day for our pilots request an invite here. [https://tilion.com]

much love. arham

story_text.value:
My friend and I have worked at a number of BI companies and thought: Can’t a coding agent do most of this now?

Almost. They just need a context/semantic layer to ensure query correctness and some kind of artifact for publishing findings and visualizations.

We built an open source project called Graphene that provides these tools:

- Semantic layer that’s more token-efficient than YAML, more deterministic than Markdown (eg, composable, callable metric macros), with a query API that’s well in-distribution (SQL). - MDX-like files for dashboards (Markdown with inlined SQL + HTML components for viz with support for CSS and Javascript) - Connects to popular data warehouses or local DuckDB

Your coding agent will build really in-depth reports and can ofc leverage any other skills or context that you've made available to it. We dogfood it inside a monorepo with our website, app source code, planning docs, etc so the agent has access to a ton of context. It’s also nice that the agent can add instrumentation, adjust pipelines and transformations, and add dashboards all in one PR.

If you want to try it out, just point your coding agent at https://github.com/graphene-data/graphene/blob/main/docs/set... and ask it to set up Graphene.

If you don’t have data to play with, you can clone our example project:

1. `git clone <https://github.com/graphene-data/example-flights.git`> 2. `cd example-flights && npm install`

Would love any/all feedback!

title.value: Show HN: Graphene – Data analysis toolkit for your coding agent

story_text.value:
I love keybr, but it only sees the ten minutes a day I spend on keybr, not the ten hours I spend typing elsewhere. Can’t improve what you don’t measure.

(A)I made Fumble is a macOS menu-bar app that watches you type (all day, all local), works out which keys/key pairs are costing you time and gives you lessons built around them.

One thing that surprised me: my slowest key is B, but the one costing me the most time is G. It's less than half as slow, but I press it three times as often. And 7 of my 10 worst key pairs start with space. I need to get better at starting words.

Some design decisions HN might want to argue with:

- I rank weak keys by time lost, not how slow they are. Time lost is how far a key is over your baseline, times how often you press it. A key 40ms slow that you hit 2k times costs more than one 220ms slow that you hit 50 times. The goal isn't to practice the slowest keys, it's to raise your WPM.

- Your baseline is the median of your own per-key p95s, not the p95 of every keystroke pooled together. Pooling lets a common slow key drag the baseline up and hide itself, and those are the keys that slow down the whole show.

- Slow finger vs thinking: pause adapts to each key pair based on your own median for that pair. There's no flat cutoff.

- The WPM figure shows you what it left out: keystrokes injected by software (text expanders, Keyboard Maestro, osascript), autorepeat, idle time and practice sessions. Every exclusion can be seen in the dropdown.

Privacy: it records physical keycodes and timings not characters. What goes to disk is counters and latency histograms, with no keystroke sequence. Also records nothing while a password field has focus. There's no network code/account/telemetry. PRIVACY.md lists the remaining risk (adjacent-pair frequencies) and gives commands to verify all of this yourself.

It can't be on the Mac App Store, because it needs Input Monitoring and the store requires sandboxing. The download is signed and notarized, so it opens like any normal Mac app.

Free and open source, written in Swift for macOS 14+.

Download: https://fumble.alexmcconnell.ie Source: https://github.com/alexiscodingbits/Fumble

Warning: early days. Not everything has been tested in the wild yet.

The thing I'd most like ideas on is word choice for the weak-spot drills. Right now it takes my top 5 weak keys and top 5 weak pairs and leans towards words that contain them. That treats every weak spot as equal, and it picks words one at a time. What I actually want is the set of 30 words that wins back the most time overall, weighted by how much each weak spot is costing me. It feels like a set-cover problem, and I'm sure there's a smarter way to do it than mine. If you've worked on anything like this, I'd love to hear how you'd approach it.

title.value: Show HN: Fumble – keybr, but it learns from everything you type (macOS)

story_text.value:
I've built a local decision engine drop-in replacement for the TypeSafe System One api because i wanted to test locally some sensitive use cases and at the time jev subscriptions was closed.

Snap supports 4 class of questions that let you classify, rank and decide about an input in sub-second on your local machine. It doesn't generate text, it reads logits in a a single forward pass.

If you have a mac you can run brew install emnlmn/snap/snap and then snap serve. It will pull the snap1-2b model from HF and start a local web server and web playground ui.

Even if the benchmarks show a 0.643 zero-shot accuracy score on zero-shot typed-decisions, snap1-2b it's 2b model, you can't expect high intelligence from it.

I'd like to share it with the community and would love to get feedback about the runtime and the training i've done with snap1. It's my first big work in the machine learning world and i hope it can be useful to someone that want to test out decision model locally.

Open weight model, MIT license.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, Anders and Tom here. We're building Magnitude, an inference engine for agents that optimizes itself to run as fast as possible on your hardware. It works on Mac, Linux, and Windows on any hardware and is up to 2x faster than llama.cpp.

We're both software engineers and previously built an open source browser agent to 4k+ GH stars and 100k+ downloads. We increasingly wanted to run it on local models, but found that no inference engine worked for our use case.

Inference engines today all make a performance tradeoff. They are either:

- Built for batched inference on datacenter hardware at the cost of single-session performance (vLLM, SGLang) - Designed for broad compatibility instead of optimizing for specific hardware (llama.cpp, Ollama) - Specialized for specific hardware or models but lacking engine completeness (oMLX, ds4)

Plus none of them are designed for running agents locally. Sessions are long, several often run at once, and you still want to use your computer for other things.

Magnitude is built for maximum performance on your hardware and running local agents:

- On-device compilation and tuning: Kernels are written with flexible parameters that are tuned on your actual device before the model runs. This gives you broad hardware compatibility with the same performance ceiling as hardware-specific kernels.

- Focus on best architectures: We write our tunable, highly efficient kernels for the most popular open-weights families. This allows us to achieve and surpass the performance of hardware or model specialized engines, without forcing ourselves to over-generalize at the cost of performance.

- Dynamic memory allocation: Magnitude reserves only enough memory up front to hold model weights. As your agent sessions grow, the memory heap dynamically increases, and frees itself when agents stop. Your hardware can still be used for other stuff while agents run.

- Hybrid paged attention: We borrow the best ideas from engines like SGLang to allow concurrent sessions to share prefix caches, but optimize placement for memory-adjacency so single-session performance doesn't suffer.

Magnitude is fully open source (Apache 2.0). We built it in Rust, including a custom GPU kernel runtime and autotuner. We take inspiration from the best innovations in inference from academics (e.g. FlashAttention, FlashInfer, TurboQuant) as well as other engines (e.g. SGLang radix attention) to reach the performance ceiling.

Benchmarked against llama.cpp with Qwen 3.6 35B A3B (4 bit), 64k context, no speculative decoding:

Metal (Mac M4 Pro 48 GB) - 92% faster decode (30 tok/s → 57 tok/s) - 9% faster prefill (466 tok/s → 507 tok/s) - 28% less per-agent memory usage

CUDA (DGX Spark) - 19% faster decode (49 tok/s → 58 tok/s) - 23% faster prefill (2,033 tok/s → 2,507 tok/s) - 27% less per-agent memory usage

Magnitude ships as a desktop app that you can easily connect with whatever agents you already use (Pi, OpenCode, Hermes, Codex, and more). It automatically runs models on demand when these agents actually need them, and shuts them down after inactivity. Here's what it looks like: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qE8BWEZu7o

We're excited to push Magnitude further to let you run bigger models on the same hardware while continuing to improve performance. Our plans include:

- Expert streaming: store experts on RAM or disk and load them just-in-time. This lets you run models bigger than what otherwise would fit on your GPU.

- Kernel compiler: our current kernels tune a few parameters to fit your hardware. We can take this further with a fully custom compiler that automatically chooses how to fuse kernels and which implementations to use, to make it fit to your hardware even better.

- Multi-device utilization: Make the best possible use of all hardware on a system (CPU, GPUs, RAM, disk) by detecting these and automatically solving for the best model layout.

We'd love for more people to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we'll be around all day!

story_text.value:
I've long been an index-investing type of person, but last year I started making some side bets, especially in tech (some inspired by WSB). I was sharing them with friends and wanted to simplify that.

This is how Investment Bets came about: you pick a ticker, a direction (long or short) and optionally a target date. The server fetches and records your entry price when you open the bet, and your exit price when you close it or reach the target date.

Each bet is scored on percentage gain/loss and has equal weight, so account size doesn't matter. The leaderboard sums your percentage results. I wanted to reward being right consistently, and since there's no compounding, a bad streak doesn't make your next good bets count for less.

The API is also open to AI agents. There's an OpenAPI file, llms.txt, Agent Skills under /.well-known and a single-file demo agent that reads headlines and places at most one bet per run. The checks that matter are in code (duplicate ticker, past target date, ticker the server can't resolve), so they don't depend on the model following the prompt. Agents get the same server-recorded prices as everyone else and show up on the same leaderboard.

https://investment-bets.com

https://investment-bets.com/agent

Please let me know if you have questions or feedback!
